summary: A bibliography of information about TCP/IP internetworking, prepared by the User Services Working Group of the IETF. It is FYI 3 and informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1175 is a reading list for people learning how the Internet works. It points to books, articles, guides, glossaries and RFCs, sorted into ten kinds of material, and adds a short note on what each one covers.

subtitle: A reading list for people starting out with computer networking.

tldr.problem: People who had just met the Internet had no reliable way to find the books, articles and manuals that explained how it worked.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF User Services Working Group collected the material, wrote a short abstract for each entry and sorted it into ten categories, from articles and books to glossaries and RFCs.
tldr.outcome: The result is FYI 3, an Informational memo that specifies no standard; its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

today: RFC 1175 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so nothing depends on it. It stands as a record of the reading list the IETF User Services Working Group published in August 1990, including instructions for downloading files that describe the distribution methods available at the time.

sections.title: Why This Bibliography Exists
sections.content:
RFC 1175 is FYI 3, a memo published in August 1990 by the User Services Working Group of the Internet Engineering Task Force. The memo says plainly that it does not specify any standard: it is a bibliography of information about TCP/IP internetworking, provided for the Internet community.

The working group formed for exactly this purpose. On 1 June 1989 several members met at the JVNC Supercomputer Center in Princeton, New Jersey, to create a group that would assemble a bibliography of useful information about the Internet for end users and for the people who help end users. The first official meeting of the User Documents Working Group was held at the Stanford IETF in July 1989. Its goal was to gather on-line and printed documents, reference materials and multimedia training tools that addressed general networking information and how to use the Internet.

The audience was beginner and intermediate level end users. The abstract describes the result as a representative collection meant to help the reader become familiar with the concepts of internetworking and to form a starting place for further research.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a reading list for people who are new to the Internet. It names the books and articles worth reading and says what each one covers, so a beginner can start somewhere sensible instead of guessing.

sections.title: How the Bibliography Is Organized
sections.content:
The bibliography is split into ten categories, each with its own section: Articles, Bibliographies, Books, Conferences and Workshops, Glossaries, Guides, Multimedia, Newsletters, Reports and Papers, and Requests for Comments.

Within a category the entries are sorted alphabetically by author or authoring organisation. The one exception is the section of RFCs, which is ordered by RFC number. Every entry carries the usual bibliographic details plus a short abstract that says what the material is about and how to obtain it. The memo warns that these abstracts are often excerpts taken verbatim from the material being described, so the wording may not be the working group's own.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is sorted into ten kinds of material, from journal articles to RFCs. Each entry gives the author and title and then a short summary, so you can tell whether a document is worth your time before you read it.

sections.title: Where the Memo Says to Start
sections.content:
For a reader who is unsure what to read first, the memo recommends Ed Krol's The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Internet, listed in the Guides section. For an introduction to the Internet protocols it names two documents: Charles Hedrick's Introduction to the Internet Protocols and Doug Comer's textbook Internetworking with TCP/IP: Principles, Protocols, and Architecture.

For guidance on the networks that already exist it points to Tracy L. LaQuey's User's Directory of Computer Networks and John S. Quarterman's The Matrix: Computer Networks and Conferencing Systems Worldwide. The memo then asks readers to scan the whole bibliography rather than stop at the first recommendation, because some items will suit a particular person's needs or a particular site better than others.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo names a first book for newcomers, two documents for understanding the protocols, and two directories for finding out which networks exist. It also asks readers to look through the whole list, not only the first entry.

sections.title: Downloading the Files with Anonymous FTP
sections.content:
Much of the material was available online, and the memo gives a worked example using the File Transfer Protocol (FTP). The user connects to the host nic.ddn.mil, logs in with the user name anonymous and types guest at the password prompt, changes into the RFC: directory, lists the files with dir or ls, fetches one with get, and leaves with quit. The memo notes that versions of the FTP program differ from system to system, so the commands shown may need to be modified to work on your own machine.

The same section records where the material sat. The DDN Network Information Center (NIC) held the central set of files, with shadow copies at MERIT and CSNET, and RFCs were fetched from it with the pathname RFC:RFCnnnn.TXT. The same host ran a mail service for sites that could not use FTP: a request sent to SERVICE@NIC.DDN.MIL with the RFC number in the subject line. The NSFNet Network Information Service did the same from NIS.NSF.NET, where the first line of the message had to read SEND RFCnnnn.TXT-1 and the subject line was left blank.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the documents could be downloaded, and the memo shows the exact commands: connect to a host, log in as anonymous, move into the RFC directory, list the files, and fetch the one you want.

sections.title: The RFC Series and Adding Entries
sections.content:
The memo's section on the RFC series explains that RFCs are the working notes of the Internet research and development community, on any topic in computer communication, from a meeting report to the specification of a standard. Anyone can submit one by electronic mail to the RFC Editor, who was Jon Postel. RFCs are not refereed publications, but they do get technical review from task forces, individual technical experts or the RFC Editor. They are distributed online as public access files, and the complete set was kept at the DDN Network Information Center at SRI International.

Two points matter for anyone finding their way through the series. A document, once it has a number, is never revised or re-issued under that number, so there is never a question of having the most recent version of an RFC. A protocol, on the other hand, may be improved and documented again in several different RFCs, which means you have to check that you hold the most recent document for a protocol. The memo points at the Internet Activities Board's IAB Official Protocol Standards, RFC 1140, issued quarterly, for the state of standardisation.

New entries for the bibliography itself were sent by electronic mail to us-wg@nnsc.nsf.net. Each proposal had to give the author or authoring organisation, the title, the publication details such as journal, volume, number and pages, the publisher, the city and date of publication, one of the material categories, and a one-paragraph abstract that also says how the material can be obtained.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo explains how RFCs themselves work: anyone can submit one, a numbered document is never reissued under the same number, and a protocol can be described again in a later RFC when it changes. It also lists the details a new bibliography entry had to include.

sections.title: What the Memo Says About Security
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is one line long: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The bibliography points at learning material rather than at risks, and it offers no analysis of authentication, privacy or the safety of the file distribution method it describes.

The memo closes with two appendices. Appendix A is a disclaimer in which the IETF, the Internet Activities Board, the United States Government and the National Science Foundation make no warranty about the accuracy, completeness or usefulness of the information, and note that the views of the authors are their own rather than the views of those bodies. Appendix B is a list of acronyms, from ARP and ASCII through EARN, FTP, IAB, IETF, IP, NSF, SMTP, SNMP and TCP, for the terms used throughout the bibliography.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says in one line that it does not discuss security. It ends with a legal disclaimer and a list of acronyms, such as FTP and TCP, for the terms it uses.

references.text: User Datagram Protocol (UDP). A Recommended Standard Protocol. Provides a datagram service to applications. Adds port addressing to the IP services.
Internet Protocol (IP). A Required Standard Protocol. The universal protocol of the Internet. This datagram protocol provides the universal addressing of hosts in the Internet.
Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP). A Required Standard Protocol. The control messages and error reports that go with the Internet Protocol.
Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). A Recommended Standard Protocol. Provides reliable end-to-end data stream service.
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP). A Recommended Standard Protocol. The procedure for transmitting computer mail between hosts.
Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol. An Elective Network Specific Standard Protocol. A procedure for finding the network hardware address corresponding to an Internet Address.
Telnet Protocol. A Recommended Standard Protocol. The protocol for remote terminal access.
Exterior Gateway Protocol. A Recommended Standard Protocol. The protocol used between gateways of different administrations to exchange routing information.
Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure. A Required Standard Protocol. Specifies procedures for the use of subnets, which are logical sub-sections of a single Internet network.

Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP). A Recommended Draft Standard Protocol. Provides an IP/UDP bootstrap protocol which allows a diskless client machine to discover its own IP address, the address of a server host, and the name of a file to be loaded into memory and executed.
File Transfer Protocol (FTP). A Recommended Standard Protocol. The protocol for moving files between Internet hosts. Provides for access control and negotiation of file parameters.

The Request for Comments Reference Guide. Provides a historical account of the Request for Comments series by categorizing and summarizing RFC numbers 1 through 999 issued between the years 1969-1987.
Official Internet Protocols. A Required Standard Memo. An official status report on the protocols used in the Internet community.
Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities. A Recommended Standard Protocol. The revised basic definition of the Domain Name System. Obsoletes RFC 882.
IAB Official Protocol Standards. Issued quarterly, describing the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet.
Krol, Ed, "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Internet", 24 pgs., University of Illinois Urbana, Urbana-Champaign, IL, September 1989.
Hedrick, Charles L., "Introduction to the Internet Protocols", 34 pgs., Rutgers University Computer Science Facilities Group, Piscataway, NJ, July 3, 1987.
Comer, Douglas E., "Internetworking with TCP/IP: Principles, Protocols, and Architecture", 382 pgs., Prentice Hall, Inc., Englewood Cliffs, NJ, 1988.
LaQuey, Tracy L., "User's Directory of Computer Networks", 653 pgs., Digital Press, Bedford, MA, May 1990.
Quarterman, John S., "The Matrix: Computer Networks and Conferencing Systems Worldwide", 746 pgs., Digital Press, Bedford, MA, 1990.
